cells.tense: You're at the shared table right now, holding your end and passing what's needed before anyone asks for it.
cells.ask: Bring one piece of your own history to the next gathering and tell it out loud, then leave it with the group without steering how it lands — see what comes back.
cells.core:
On an ordinary week you bring the dish, you take the call, you're in the room when the group needs hands. You carry your part of what's held in common and pass it along, and the people near you feel the weight as shared rather than carried alone.

What's still open is direction. Holding the line for the group is a craft you already have; choosing which way the group walks next is a different move, and it happens out loud. Putting one of your own stories into the keeping — not the group's, yours — points the room at something and gives your voice its own weight in it. What that gives back is a say in where this goes.
cells.sheetLine: You carry your part of this and hand it on without being asked.
cells.verb: passing your strength on to the people who need it, keeping the shared things going
cells.place: inside the customs and stories one group hands down to the next

cells.tense: You're leaning into a day that hasn't come, and your hands have gone tight around the shared things.
cells.ask: Pick one shared thing you're holding — the group chat, the meals, the person people check on — and leave it be for a week, saying nothing about why.
cells.core:
Most weeks you read the room and move before a word is said. You know whose week is heavy and you're there, and that's what makes the group gather around you rather than around a schedule.

Lately the moving happens early — guarding against something that hasn't arrived and gripping the shared things harder than they need. Setting one piece down for a week isn't quitting it. It's finding out whether it stands with your hand off it, which is the only way to learn what it can hold on its own. What you get back is the difference between what needs you and what only got used to you.
cells.sheetLine: You're bracing against a need no one has named yet, and your grip shows it.

cells.tense: You stepped away from the telling a while back, and you're still standing at the doorway that closed behind you.
cells.ask: Take one small thing that belongs to the group — a recipe, a name, a phrase — and hand it to one person this week, even awkwardly, even in a sentence.
cells.core:
When support runs well in a group's shared life, it sounds ordinary. You show up, you say the person's name at the table, you make the dish that gets made every year, and the strength of the whole moves through your hands alongside the others'.

In the group's life you know the strength is still circulating — the meals still happen, the birthdays still get marked — while your own hands have gone still at the edge of it. Picking up one thing that's already yours to give is smaller than returning. Do it once, to one person, before you decide anything larger, and it starts to show you what your part in this still is.

cells.tense: You're already keeping the shared stories going and putting resources where they're needed, and you name the group as the one doing it.
cells.ask: This week say out loud that one thing you keep alive is yours — the meal, the call, the telling — and let the sentence sit in the room.
cells.core:
On a normal week you're one of the hands the group's strength runs through. You keep the memory, you bring what's needed, you show up at the gathering and stay to stack the chairs — and the room keeps running on that whether or not anyone says so.

The unclaimed part is yours to take. The work you do sits where it can happen quietly, and it does, so nobody has told you it's yours. Saying one piece is yours doesn't make it more real. It puts it back in your own hands, where the next thing you choose to keep can be chosen on purpose.

attempts.check: The card says nothing about the person; my only unsupported moves would be guesses about what happened at the table or why the stories stopped, so none of those are in the cells. A reader could say 'I haven't stopped; I just don't want to talk about it' — the cells name the condition as what they do with the telling, not as who they are, so that objection still leaves them something to try. The asks survive being wrong: they are physical and public, and would teach the person something about the table even if my read is off. The sentence that serves the writer is the sheet line about carrying stories alone — rewritten so it hands back authorship instead of diagnosing it.
